title: Final Advice and a Farewell
overview: The letter closes with practical advice on love, money and leaders, a last picture of Jesus dying outside the city, and personal greetings.

parts.label: Love that shows up (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The readers are urged to keep caring for one another, to welcome strangers (Abraham once hosted visitors who turned out to be angels), and to stand by prisoners as if chained beside them. They are also told to stay faithful in marriage and free of greed, leaning on God's old promise to Joshua and Israel never to leave or abandon them.

parts.label: Remember who led you (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: The first leaders who taught them had likely died by now, perhaps some for their faith, and the readers are told to look at how those lives ended and copy their trust. Jesus, the one those leaders relied on, has not changed and is still there for this new generation.

parts.label: Grace, not food rules (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: The writer warns against teachings that tie spiritual strength to eating or avoiding certain foods, though scholars are unsure exactly which food practices are meant. The altar believers eat from is usually read as Jesus' death, which the writer says those still serving the old sanctuary do not share in.

parts.label: Outside the camp (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: On the yearly day for clearing the people's sins, the high priest carried animal blood into the sanctuary's innermost room, while the bodies were burned outside the camp. Jesus likewise died outside Jerusalem's walls, and the readers are invited to join him there, accepting the shame of being outsiders while they wait for a lasting city still to come.

parts.label: The offerings that remain (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: In place of animal offerings, the gifts God welcomes now are praise spoken openly and practical generosity toward others. The readers are asked to trust their current leaders, who will answer to God for how they cared for them.

parts.label: Prayer, blessing and goodbyes (vv. 18-25)
parts.note: The writer asks for prayer to be reunited with them soon and prays that God, who raised Jesus as the great shepherd, will equip them to do good. Timothy has been set free, probably from prison, and greetings come from people from Italy, which could mean the writer was in Italy or among Italians living elsewhere.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether going to Jesus outside the camp was mainly a call for these first readers to break with temple worship, or a broader call for any believer to accept being an outsider in their own society.
think: What makes it easier or harder for you to welcome someone you don't know?
